title: Horizontal scaling
idea: Horizontal scaling means adding more machines that run the same app, with a load balancer spreading requests across them, so capacity grows by adding servers.

analogy.text: A supermarket opening more checkout lanes. Each cashier works the same way, and a host points each shopper to a free lane.
analogy.breaks: Shoppers carry their own basket; servers must not hold your data.

points: A load balancer receives every request and picks one server for it.
Any server may handle any request, so servers must be stateless.
Shared state moves out of the process into a database or cache.
Adding or losing a server changes capacity without changing the app.

steps.caption: Clients send every request to one address: the load balancer.
The load balancer sends the first request to server 1.
The next request may go to server 2. Each server must handle it the same way.
A later request may reach server 3. No server can rely on having seen this user before.
Sessions, counters and uploads live in the shared store, so every server sees the same data.

pitfalls: Do not keep sessions in server memory; the next request may hit another server.
Do not save uploads to local disk; store them in shared object storage.
Do not count in a process variable; each server keeps its own total.

quiz.q: Three servers sit behind a load balancer. Each keeps a request counter in a variable. What does that counter show?
options: The total requests across all three servers
Only the requests that one server handled
Nothing; counters reset on every request
The same value on every server
quiz.why: Each process has its own memory. A counter in a variable counts only its own server's requests; use a shared store for totals.

takeaway: Scale out by adding stateless servers, and keep shared state outside them.
